newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian capital tackles plague of stray dogs.
newsitem.headline: Romanian capital tackles plague of stray dogs.

text.p: Bucharest's city hall on Wednesday presented a mass sterilisation plan to reduce by three-quarters the Romanian capital's 200,000-strong stray dog population, which overruns parks, rubbish tips and even airport runways.

"Of more than 200,000 dogs in Bucharest, only 25 percent will be left in five years when our programme ends," city councillor Mihai Voiculescu told a news conference. "This is a correct canine ecological balance for a modern capital city."
Packs of dogs rummaging through rubbish bins, harassing passers-by or barking at moving cars have invaded virtually every corner of the city of 2.3 million.
Many roam the runways at Otopeni international airport, one of many sponsors of the programme expected to cost the equivalent of $1.3 million.

Officials say many thousands of strays descended from dogs turned loose during Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's rapid demolition of city centre homes in the late 1980s to make way for his grandiose "House of the People" palace.
Starting next week, 30 dog catchers authorised to nab dogs only with their bare hands will fan out through the capital to bring in strays to designated clinics.
Vets working free of charge will sterilise, vaccinate, de-infest the dogs and fit them with identification collars.

"The dogs -- sterilised and marked -- will be declared community dogs protected by law," Voiculescu said. "Unfortunately we will have to put them back on the street temporarily until we can build new shelters. We can only hold 250 at the moment."

The programme was set up in response to pleas from animal rights groups to tackle the problem of the growing canine population. Statistics show one in 10 dies a violent death -- either by poisoning or being hit by cars.

Animal lovers in Romania and abroad bombarded authorities with protests after seeing television pictures of previous attempts to curb the dog population -- by poisoning them with strychnine and leaving them to die a limb-jerking death.
"Having in mind the universal declaration of animals' rights and other international laws, from now on we will help and protect these dogs, not kill them," Voiculescu said.

The average stray has a shorter lifespan than most pets as it lacks a guaranteed food source and is more prone to accidents or poisoning. Many strays are already elderly, so authorities hope the sterilisation plan will bring down numbers quickly.
